column2: GOLD grades by post-bronchodilator FEV1: 1 ≥ 80%, 2 50–79% (moderate), 3 30–49%, 4 < 30%. FEV1 62% is moderate.
Smoking cessation is the only measure that slows FEV1 decline in COPD and improves survival; offer varenicline/NRT with support.
Maintenance oral steroids are not used in COPD (no benefit, many harms); short courses only. Roflumilast and azithromycin reduce exacerbations.
COPD does not cause clubbing (look for cancer, bronchiectasis or fibrosis). Polycythaemia, cor pulmonale and pneumothorax are complications.
Asthma often begins before age 5 (most persistent cases), can start at any age, and is characteristically variable.
Dilated thick-walled central upper-lobe bronchi (signet ring) in a long-standing asthmatic suggest ABPA with bronchiectasis; check IgE and Aspergillus serology.
Worsening every April–May with sensitisation to oilseed rape and grass pollen is seasonal allergic asthma; optimise ICS before the season.
FEV1 rises 600 mL (23%) and the ratio normalises: a reversible obstructive defect; ≥ 400 mL strongly favours asthma.
PEF 53% of best with nocturnal symptoms in pregnancy is an exacerbation: prednisolone 40–50 mg ≥ 5 days; continue all asthma drugs.
Uncontrolled on fixed ICS/LABA + SABA: switch to ICS–formoterol MART; if still uncontrolled with eosinophilia, refer for a biologic.
Serial PEF (≥ 4×/day for 3–4 weeks, at and away from work) is the first-line test for occupational asthma.
Atopy (IgE sensitisation to common allergens) is the strongest identifiable risk factor for asthma.
Asthma severity tends to stay constant within an individual (mild rarely becomes severe), though control fluctuates.
Fatal asthma shows mucus plugs, eosinophilic airway inflammation, oedema, smooth-muscle hypertrophy and basement membrane thickening; alveoli are spared.
Asthma needs symptoms plus objective variability: FEV1 rise ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL after bronchodilator (here 300 mL, 18%).
SABA-only treatment is no longer advised; mild asthma uses as-needed low-dose budesonide–formoterol (cuts severe exacerbations by ~two-thirds).
Asthma in pregnancy follows the rule of thirds; continue ICS and relievers, as uncontrolled asthma is the real fetal risk.
Brown mucus plugs with eosinophilia in severe asthma suggest ABPA: total IgE (often > 1000) with Aspergillus-specific IgE first.
A silent chest means almost no airflow: a life-threatening feature signalling impending respiratory failure; urgent ICU review.
Asthma is obstructive: FEV1 falls more than FVC (ratio < 0.70), with reversibility. Low FVC with normal ratio means restriction.
Pulsus paradoxus up to 10 mmHg is normal, so 5 mmHg predicts a benign course; silent chest, hypercapnia and confusion are ominous.
Asthma's defining feature is reversible obstruction: FEV1 rise ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL after bronchodilator.
Obstruction with a 400 mL bronchodilator response in a young man is asthma; frequent symptoms need low-dose ICS–formoterol MART.
In acute asthma PaCO2 should be low; acidosis (pH 7.33) means tiring with CO2 retention — the strongest indication for intubation.
Silent chest and a 'normal' (rising) PaCO2 are life-threatening: give IV magnesium 1.2–2 g, continue nebulisers and get ICU review.
Obstruction with hyperinflation but normal TLCO/KCO in a never-smoker with seasonal wheeze is asthma; emphysema lowers gas transfer.
Obstruction with a low peak flow and cat exposure in a 25-year-old is asthma; confirm with FeNO or reversibility.
Chronic bronchitis is a productive cough on most days for ≥ 3 months in 2 consecutive years (MRC definition).
Steroids in a COPD exacerbation do improve FEV1 and shorten recovery, so that statement is false; antibiotics for purulent sputum.
Chronic productive cough, dyspnoea, pursed-lip breathing and barrel chest in a heavy smoker is COPD; confirm FEV1/FVC < 0.70.
Emphysema destroys elastin; loss of elastic recoil collapses small airways in expiration, causing dynamic hyperinflation on exertion.
Upper-lobe low-attenuation areas without walls are centrilobular emphysema; it can cause breathlessness and low TLCO before spirometry changes.
Persistent breathlessness on a LAMA: escalate to LABA + LAMA (GOLD 2025). ICS only with exacerbations and eosinophils ≥ 300/µL.
Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis causing restriction; asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis and emphysema are obstructive.
Frequent exacerbator despite optimal inhalers: azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly (check ECG, LFTs, hearing). Roflumilast is the alternative.
Smoking, occupational dust and biomass smoke cause COPD; adult respiratory infections trigger exacerbations but are not proven causes.
In acute hypercapnic COPD failure, NIV roughly halves mortality and reduces intubation.
ABG is the key first test in a COPD admission: detects hypercapnia/acidosis and guides controlled oxygen and NIV.
Hypoxaemic COPD exacerbation: start controlled oxygen (24–28% Venturi) to SpO2 88–92% while the ABG is taken.
Chronic foul purulent sputum, clubbing and bilateral crackles in a child suggests bronchiectasis from cystic fibrosis; sweat test.
HRCT confirms bronchiectasis: bronchi wider than the artery (signet ring), no tapering, airways within 1 cm of pleura.
CF exacerbation: antibiotics guided by recent sputum (often IV ceftazidime + tobramycin for 14 days) plus physiotherapy.
Sweat chloride ≥ 60 mmol/L (repeated) with a compatible picture is diagnostic of CF; 30–59 is intermediate.
Haemophilus influenzae is the commonest bacterial cause of infective COPD exacerbations (then pneumococcus, Moraxella).
Non-infective COPD exacerbation (sputum unchanged): prednisolone 30 mg for 5 days and more bronchodilator; antibiotics only if purulent.
COPD still breathless on SABA without asthmatic features: add LABA + LAMA (NICE NG115, GOLD 2025).
Respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa) persisting despite optimal therapy is the indication for NIV.
A chronic smoker with ABG showing acidosis, hypercapnia and raised bicarbonate has an acute-on-chronic type 2 failure from a COPD exacerbation.
